analysis.one_liner: Drops the Clean Water Act permit for spraying approved pesticides into waterways.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 256-165 on May 24, 2017, with 25 Democrats joining 231 Republicans, but the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee never acted on it before the session ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a pesticide approved under federal pesticide law is applied directly into lakes, rivers, or streams, current rules require both that approval and a water-discharge permit from the EPA or a state. This bill would eliminate the second requirement: no discharge permit whenever the pesticide itself is federally approved. Permits would still be needed for spraying that violates the pesticide rules, for stormwater, and for industrial, sewage, and ship discharges [S2, S3, S4, S5]. Supporters say the permit is duplicative paperwork; the trade-off is that routine, lawful spraying into public waters would no longer need a discharge-specific permit.
analysis.who_benefits: Pesticide applicators and the industries that use them: farms, mosquito-control districts, forestry operators, and the pesticide makers whose products are applied. They would avoid the cost and paperwork of Clean Water Act discharge permits, keeping only the product-registration rules they already face.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the EPA or state permit requirement under the Clean Water Act for discharging a FIFRA-approved pesticide into navigable waters [S2, S3, S4].

Keeps permit requirements only for narrower cases: applications that violate pesticide rules in ways that worsen water pollution, stormwater, and industrial, treatment-works, and vessel discharges [S3, S4, S5].

analysis.who_pays: People who swim in, fish, or draw drinking water from lakes, rivers, and streams that receive pesticide residues. They would lose the site-specific limits, monitoring, and public enforcement that discharge permits provide, leaving only enforcement of the pesticide product's label.

drawbacks.text: NPDES permits are where discharge-specific limits, monitoring, and citizen enforcement live under the Clean Water Act; removing them for approved-pesticide spraying leaves only label enforcement, which is not tailored to any particular waterway [S2, S3].

Supporters' best case: the permit duplicates FIFRA, which already screens each product for safety before it can be sold or used, and the bill's own exceptions show the authors did not want to shield misuse [S3, S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The paperwork relief for applicators is real, and the bill is narrower than a blanket exemption because it keeps permits for violations and for industrial and vessel discharges. But the cost is that lawful routine spraying into public waters would no longer face any discharge-specific check — no permit conditions, no monitoring, no avenue under the Clean Water Act for a community to challenge a particular application. The savings for applicators come directly out of water-quality oversight.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House on a 256-165 vote, but the Senate committee it was sent to never took it up before the Congress ended, so it never became law.

narrative.text: Introduced in February 2017 and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure and Agriculture Committees [S7].
The House Agriculture Committee ordered it reported and reported it with H. Rept. 115-131 on May 18, 2017 [S7].

A motion by Rep. McGovern to send the bill back with an instruction to bar its application where a pesticide maker had made political contributions to officials regulating it failed 183-230, with 228 of 237 House Republicans voting no [S7, S8].
Amendments by Reps. Esty and Huffman were rejected during floor consideration [S7].
The House passed the bill 256-165: 231 of 237 Republicans and 25 of 193 Democrats in favor [S9, S7].
The Senate received it on May 25, 2017, and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, where it sat with no further action through the end of the 115th Congress [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Communities and water users keep the Clean Water Act discharge permit safeguard for pesticide spraying, which the bill would have removed. Pesticide applicators and manufacturers gained nothing from the outcome; they remain subject to both product registration and discharge permitting.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Water users kept the permit safeguard

sides.party_line_note: On final passage, 231 of 237 House Republicans voted yes versus only 25 of 193 Democrats; the 25 Democratic yes votes give it a bipartisan tint, but the vote otherwise split by party.

industries.industry: Pesticide applicators (farmers, mosquito-control districts, forestry operators)
industries.note: They would no longer need Clean Water Act discharge permits for approved-pesticide spraying into waterways, saving permit costs and paperwork. The savings come from dropping discharge-specific limits and monitoring on the waters people use.

Their customers would face less permitting friction, and their products would remain governed only by FIFRA registration when applied to water. Product registration would remain the sole regulatory gate.
They would bear more pesticide residues in source waters without any permit-based monitoring or enforceable limits on the discharges.
